We need to talk about markets, and the way people feel about them.

You may have heard that Standard Chartered is preparing to replace a large number of its staff with AI in what the bank is calling a "profitability drive". The people being let go are the back-office staff, the junior analysts, the operations clerks, the men and women in the call centres in Birmingham (and Manila, and Chennai) who answer the bank's phone for it. To this crop of the soon-to-be-unemployed, Standard Chartered has referred with a unique phrase. "Lower-value human capital."

I'm a pro-market guy, and I am that seven days a week. How could I not be? Any honest reading of history will tell you that open markets, private enterprise and the right to make and keep a profit are the most successful engines of human freedom, prosperity and self-actualisation our species has ever managed to build. They are the foundation of more or less everything Britain has ever done well.

But when I read financiers referring to people about to be put out of a job as "lower-value human capital", I feel a little pang of sympathy with the Eat the Rich crowd. 

And it's not even the event itself that concerns me most, though it does, but the phrase itself. The phrase matters because, beyond its simply offensive character, there's something in it that you can see exhibited in multiple quarters these days - not just among financiers, but within governments, and among captains of industry - that's responsible for driving people to the kind of barren extremes of belief that have become so common in our world in the past decade.

Consider, for instance, the things that have been said lately on daytime TV and during spring graduation ceremonies at American universities about AI and its effect on work and the economy. 

We've seen, in those places, heads and VIP shareholders of major AI companies walk into halls full of 20-yr-olds and explain, in tones that leave these very wealthy men powerless to hide their giddy excitement, that the technology they own is going to eliminate the entry-level professions those graduates have just spent three years training for.

That white-collar work, as a viable rung on the career ladder, is finished.

That the economies the graduates will live in will become more stratified as a result of AI's inexorable expansion, if they exist at all. 

And that the graduates, on hearing all this, should consider themselves privileged, for they shall be the first to "serve" this extraordinary new technology, which of course primarily means serving the men who own it.

Now, I do not begrudge these people their breakthrough.  I build systems with AI in them for a living. I've built LLM architectures by hand, on my own. I understand the technology well-enough to grasp that it is going to be very important even if its powers have been oversold. And Britain should be building AI. In fact, our successes in the field are one of the few genuinely hopeful chapters in the British industrial story of the last decade. 

Nevertheless, there is a difference between building a powerful technology and announcing, in tones of nakedly anticipatory delight, that you intend to use it to turn the coming generations into a mass serf-class. That many of them will be immiserated and left completely without any stake in the society they live in, but that that is a price you are willing to pay in return for your unimaginable shareholder benefit. 

Talking to people like this, promising them their own ruin, is the sort of consummately moronic communication that makes people want to firebomb your house and burn down the cities they live in.

And this is a critical problem for anyone who cares about politics in the Western world, and particularly those who care about forging a new vision of broadly shared progress that is, at its base, founded on principles of trade and markets.

The problem is that people hate markets, industry, technology and the people behind them in this country and across the West because, for forty years, those people have shown that they are not even slightly interested in the notion of giving the wider population a stake in their own futures. 

And the more the captains of industry and finance gloat that the future belongs only to them, and the less anyone at any level is concerned about how we give people a stake in the future in question, the more the Mangionification of society will continue.

A doctrine for the organisation of society that does not put some kind of shared prosperity and human development at its centre is worthless.

A country whose ordinary people are told, decade after decade, that yes, you are the lower-value human capital - the future has been planned without reference to their interests, and your only pleasure is to serve those who have planned it thus - will ultimately light itself on fire. 

We must be pro-markets, pro-industry and pro-technology. But we must, at all times, also put those instruments in the service of the interests of human development. 

We must be determined that the productive engines of, for instance, this country are built so that ordinary British people own a piece of them, work inside them, profit from them, and have a future as a result of the labour they yield. 

Building powerful industries and giving ordinary people a stake in them are not two separate projects, but are one and the same project, conducted at the same time, or it is no project worth a vote. Not Britain nor the world will survive another forty years of a model in which a small caste hoovers the value upward and explains, on the way out, that the people whose jobs they took had it coming.
